strategy_title: TF32 input_precision Flag Has No Effect on Tiny Underutilized Kernels
strategy_description: Adding input_precision='tf32' to tl.dot calls produced zero measurable improvement: Compute (SM) Throughput remained at 0.29%, Duration barely changed (23.42 µs → 23.26 µs, within noise), and all occupancy/scheduler metrics were statistically identical. The kernel is so severely underutilized (0.01 waves/SM, grid=4 vs 132 SMs, achieved occupancy=3.12%) that the compute path is never the bottleneck — the kernel finishes in ~900 SM active cycles regardless of FP32 vs TF32 precision. Furthermore, L2 Compression Input Sectors increased from 736 to 916, suggesting TF32 may have introduced slightly more memory traffic. When a kernel's compute throughput is near 0% and the grid cannot fill even 1% of available SMs, switching to higher-throughput compute instructions (TF32, FP16 Tensor Cores) provides no benefit because the bottleneck is launch overhead and grid underutilization, not arithmetic throughput.
slow_pseudocode:
# BEFORE: default FP32 precision
acc = tl.dot(combined_tile, w_tile, acc=acc)
# Compute (SM) Throughput: 0.29%, Duration: 23.42 µs, Grid: 4 blocks / 132 SMs
fast_pseudocode:
# AFTER: TF32 precision flag added
acc = tl.dot(combined_tile, w_tile, acc=acc, input_precision='tf32')
# Compute (SM) Throughput: 0.29% (unchanged), Duration: 23.26 µs (noise), Grid: 4 blocks / 132 SMs
applicable_when: Never applicable when Compute (SM) Throughput is near 0% and the kernel grid is far below the SM count (waves_per_sm << 0.1). TF32/Tensor Core precision changes only help when the kernel is actually compute-bound (Compute SOL > 20%) and arithmetic throughput is the limiting factor.
do_not_apply_when: Do not apply TF32 input_precision when: (1) Compute (SM) Throughput < 5%, indicating the kernel is not compute-bound; (2) waves_per_sm < 0.1, meaning the grid cannot fill the GPU and launch overhead dominates; (3) SM Active Cycles are very low (< 1000 cycles), meaning the kernel completes too quickly for compute precision to matter. In these cases, the bottleneck is grid underutilization, not arithmetic throughput, and precision changes have no effect.
framework_notes: In Triton, input_precision='tf32' on tl.dot routes the matrix multiply through Tensor Cores with reduced mantissa precision (10 bits vs 23 bits for FP32). This only provides speedup when the kernel is actually compute-bound. On H200 with 132 SMs, a grid of 4 blocks (0.01 waves/SM) means 99% of SMs are idle — no amount of per-SM compute throughput improvement can overcome this fundamental underutilization. The fix for this kernel class is to increase grid size (more blocks), not to improve per-block arithmetic efficiency.

strategy_title: Autotune Config Swap (BLOCK_N 64→128) Yields No Improvement
strategy_description: Swapping autotune configs from BLOCK_N=64 to BLOCK_N=128 (while keeping num_stages=3-4 and BLOCK_K=64) produced essentially no change in any profiling metric: duration moved from 23.42 µs to 23.14 µs (~1.2%), all occupancy, stall, and throughput metrics were statistically identical. The profiling data shows the kernel selected the same effective config (registers=95, smem=43 KB, grid=4, achieved occupancy=3.12%) before and after, meaning the autotuner either selected the same BLOCK_N=64 config or the BLOCK_N=128 config performed identically due to the tiny problem size (M=8, N=256). The reported 0.5752x speedup is a benchmark-level regression unrelated to the GPU kernel metrics, likely due to autotuning overhead or measurement noise. Adding allow_tf32=True to tl.dot had no measurable effect on compute throughput (Compute SM Throughput remained at 0.29%), confirming that TF32 Tensor Cores are not engaged at this problem scale or that the kernel is not compute-bound.

These changes cannot improve latency when the bottleneck is grid underutilization, not arithmetic throughput. Also note: TF32 was previously flagged as a correctness risk (max_diff~40 in prior attempts per memory item b747dbda); this iteration's near-zero GPU metric change suggests the autotuner may have avoided the BLOCK_N=128 config entirely.

strategy_title: Autotune Config Swap (BLOCK_N 64→128) Yields No GPU Improvement
strategy_description: Swapping autotune configs to replace BLOCK_K=128 variants with BLOCK_N=128 variants (while keeping num_stages=3-4) produced zero measurable GPU metric improvement: all profiling metrics before and after are statistically identical (duration 23.26 µs vs 23.23 µs, grid=4, registers=95, smem=43 KB, achieved occupancy=3.12%, warp cycles/instruction 4.47 vs 4.49, No Eligible 77.66% vs 77.56%). The plan also intended to eliminate clone() via ping-pong double-buffering in the Python wrapper, but the actual diff only modified the @triton.autotune config lists — the Python wrapper loop was not changed. When a kernel is severely underutilized (0.01 waves/SM, 4 blocks on 132 SMs), autotune config reshuffling (BLOCK_N, BLOCK_K, num_warps variations) cannot improve performance because the bottleneck is grid underutilization and launch overhead, not per-block tile efficiency. The 0.573x speedup is benchmark-level noise unrelated to GPU kernel metrics.

applicable_when: Never: reshuffling autotune configs (swapping BLOCK_N=64 for BLOCK_N=128, or BLOCK_K=64 for BLOCK_K=128) on a kernel with grid=4 blocks and 0.01 waves/SM produces no measurable improvement. The autotuner selects the same effective config (registers=95, smem=43 KB) regardless of which BLOCK_N/BLOCK_K variants are offered when the problem size is tiny and the grid cannot fill the GPU.
do_not_apply_when: Do not apply autotune config reshuffling (BLOCK_N expansion, BLOCK_K swap) when: (1) the kernel grid is far below SM count (waves_per_sm < 0.1); (2) all occupancy and stall metrics are already at their floor (achieved occupancy=3.12%, no-eligible~77%); (3) the intended optimization (e.g., clone elimination, double-buffering) requires Python wrapper changes but the diff only modifies the @triton.autotune config list. Config-only diffs cannot implement wrapper-level optimizations. This is now the fourth consecutive iteration where autotune config reshuffling alone failed to improve this kernel.
framework_notes: In Triton, @triton.autotune config list changes only affect which tile configuration is selected at runtime. They cannot implement Python-wrapper-level optimizations such as ping-pong double-buffering or clone() elimination. If the plan calls for modifying the for-loop body in the Python wrapper, the diff must show changes to that loop body — not just to the @triton.autotune decorator. Verify the diff is non-empty and targets the correct code region before concluding the plan was applied. This is the same failure mode as items exp_batch_h2o_timesteps_empty_diff_regression_003 and exp_autotune_config_swap_block_k_expansion_no_improvement_004.
